Open ASR Leaderboard: Trends and Insights with Fresh Multilingual & Long-Form Tracks

📅 21 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show.
  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • It has been revealed that over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

It has been revealed that over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the major takeaways 👇.

Models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders at the moment lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

While highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

Recent findings suggest that for even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

According to recent reports, openAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

That said, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are at the moment benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for fresh dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

Recent findings suggest that 🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

Recent findings suggest that for long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Recent findings suggest that among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

It has been revealed that the tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

According to recent reports, when fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a fresh adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

Industry observers note that rapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more promptly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Industry observers note that transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

The problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

For developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an important part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

These are two different events.

In a recent development, when an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:.

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy problems.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three important states:.

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

According to recent reports, these distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the vital stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:.

This example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another important area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:.

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Common configuration mistakes include:.

Forgetting to authorize a new email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Exceeding SPF's DNS lookup limit.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

Industry observers note that remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A failed DKIM check might indicate:.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Message modification after signing.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:.

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement plan.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after people report a problem.

A useful testing sequence includes:.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The vital point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

It allows developers to examine:.

Email subject lines and headers.

Embedded images and attachments.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a newly introduced user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production owners.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

The application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:.

Retries are particularly important, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

In a recent development, also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is crucial, but it cannot reveal every matter that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

These tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking key details.

Before releasing a latest email feature, review the following:.

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Check the SMTP or API response.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Test links and personalized content.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Test queue failures and retry behavior.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

#57893. Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1420 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI.
  • Sources indicate that the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

Sources indicate that the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

In a recent development, we learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

Over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

Long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

It has been revealed that using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

According to recent reports, ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

Industry observers note that this approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Sources indicate that building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these problems.

A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

From our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created new failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

Industry observers note that we used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Sources indicate that rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

In a recent development, what is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

A great insight on getting more by doing less.

Tech Report: What Actually Happens When a Kafka Region Fails?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that most Kafka deployments in the industry plan to survive the loss of a single Kafka broker or an availability zone. But that's not enough for critical Tier-0 infrastructure where downtime or data loss of even a few seconds could have a massive business impact.

Recent findings suggest that in such scenarios, the failure model should consider not just the loss of a broker or a zone, but the loss of an entire region. The business is expected to operate without interruption even when a whole region goes down, and it should be possible to also roll the cluster safely while operating in that state, to apply any break-glass changes.

According to recent reports, but what actually happens inside Kafka when an entire region goes down? What happens to the replicas, producer writes, and KRaft quorum? And what happens when that region comes back?

Let's walk through these scenarios using a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka architecture.

For a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster, we need three different regions with isolated failure domains and a minimum of two brokers in each region.

Brokers in each region should be configured with rack awareness to indicate their failure domains as follows:.

For Tier-0 workloads, each topic's partitions should be configured to have a replication factor (RF) of 6. Kafka's rack-aware replica assignment will spread the replicas across the three regions. If the automatic replica assignment doesn't allocate two replicas per region, we have to explicitly reassign replicas immediately after topic creation to meet our availability guarantees.

This way, if one region goes down entirely, we still have four replicas surviving and the cluster would still continue to operate.

But just running brokers in multiple regions is not the solution here. In fact, that's the easy part. The hard question is, what guarantee remains when one of those regions disappears, and does it solve the business needs?

Let's say Region A goes down entirely.

The two brokers in that region become unavailable, leaving four surviving replicas across Regions B and C.

For any partitions whose leaders were in Region A, Kafka needs to elect upcoming leaders from the surviving in-sync replicas.

But having four surviving replicas alone does not determine whether Kafka will continue accepting writes.

Industry observers note that the next step is to define what is considered a successful write in this Kafka setup. For this, we need two configs:.

min.insync.replicas determines the minimum number of replicas that should be present in the in-sync replica set (ISR) of a partition for Kafka to accept writes when producers use acks=all.

acks=all is a producer-side config that ensures that the producer will get an acknowledgment only when the write has been successfully replicated to the required in-sync replicas.

These two settings work together to satisfy the durability guarantees we want.

When all three regions are healthy, ISR would include all six replicas. Let's say one region goes down, then the ISR would drop down to four.

Since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

There may be temporary interruptions while Kafka detects the failure, elects new leaders, and clients reconnect to them. But once the surviving leaders are available, the cluster can continue accepting writes as long as the ISR requirements are met.

The goal isn't availability at any cost, but rather the system should be available as long as the durability guarantees that we designed for can be maintained.

Now let's make the scenario more interesting.

Industry observers note that region A is still down. We have four replicas surviving across Regions B and C.

What if we need to roll the cluster one broker at a time, to apply any break-glass changes?

During that time, the ISR can go down from four to three. But since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

Let's look at how the cluster behaves under different failure scenarios.

Kafka will stop accepting writes only when the surviving ISR drops below three.

This is an crucial distinction for Tier-0 workloads.

It's not sufficient to design a cluster that survives a region failure. We also need to consider whether the cluster can continue operating safely while already in that degraded state.

It has been revealed that so far, we focused on the data plane. Now switching gears, the KRaft controllers have a completely different availability model.

They form the metadata quorum, and a majority is needed to continue operation.

For our setup, five controllers could be distributed as 2 + 2 + 1 across the three regions, requiring a majority of three to maintain quorum.

If either of the regions containing two controllers goes down, three controllers remain. If the region containing one controller goes down, four remain.

So, the controller quorum survives the loss of any one region.

But, unlike brokers, we cannot necessarily roll the controllers at that point because taking one controller down could cause the quorum to drop below three.

In a recent development, with a static quorum, one way to solve this is to use more controllers, and a 3 + 3 + 3 distribution would provide this. Losing one region would leave six controllers with room to still roll the controllers, as we only need five to maintain quorum.

On the flip side, an increase in quorum size also increases the coordination overhead. The official Kafka documentation typically recommends three or five controllers, which tolerate one or two concurrent failures respectively.

Alternatively, with dynamic KRaft quorum (KIP-853), introduced in Kafka 3.9, we can add or remove controllers from the voting quorum without restarting the cluster.

It has been revealed that for example, with our 2 + 2 + 1 setup, if a region containing two controllers goes down, the remaining three controllers can still maintain quorum. We can then remove the failed controllers from the voting membership, one at a time, reducing the quorum size to three. This allows us to roll one of the surviving controllers while still maintaining the new majority of two.

In a recent development, however, dynamic quorum reconfiguration is not automatic. The surviving controllers must be able to maintain quorum and successfully commit the membership changes before we can proceed with the controller restart.

You need to consider whether you want the same availability guarantee for the controllers as that of the data plane, and whether dynamic quorum reconfiguration during a regional outage is acceptable for your Tier-0 workloads.

So far, we assumed that a region either works or goes down completely.

But the WAN itself becomes a failure mode.

In this setup, a partly working WAN between two regions can be more dangerous than a link that's completely down.

Increased latency, packet loss, or intermittent connectivity complications between regions can cause replication to lag, ultimately resulting in replicas falling out of ISR.

The three regions might be independently healthy, but if the connectivity between them is not, then the availability of the cluster might be impacted.

Going back to the CAP theorem, to tolerate a network partition, we must choose between consistency and availability.

So, if a partition's ISR falls below the configured min.insync.replicas of three due to a network partition, Kafka stops accepting writes with acks=all rather than weakening those guarantees.

Similarly, if the KRaft controller quorum is lost, then no metadata changes, like leader elections, can happen in the cluster, even though existing data-plane traffic may continue for some time.

The availability guarantees we discussed also come with their own costs.

Sources indicate that the first cost is client latency. With cross-region replication and acks=all, the network latency between these regions directly affects producer latency. Consumers can also pay the WAN latency cost when consuming from partition leaders located in a different region.

It has been revealed that the second cost is replication overhead. With RF=6, there is additional storage, network traffic, and replication-related coordination cost in the brokers compared to a smaller number of replicas.

So, in an architecture like this, monitoring the health of the network paths between these regions is as critical as monitoring the Kafka brokers and controllers.

Metrics like round-trip latency (RTT) between regions, packet loss, TCP retransmissions, connection errors/timeouts, and network throughput/bandwidth utilization are a good start.

When one region goes down, all the partition leaders in that region would move to the two other surviving regions.

This implies that those two regions would have to handle more producer and consumer traffic, network throughput, and disk I/O.

Even if the cluster is designed to satisfy its ISR and controller quorum requirements, if it's not sized to handle these failures when one region goes down, the surviving regions would be overloaded, resulting in higher latencies, timeouts, and operational instability.

So, for Tier-0 infrastructure, capacity planning should always be done for failure states and not stop at normal operations.

Now let's say Region A comes back online.

The brokers in the recovered region might have to catch up on a significant amount of data before they become fully in sync again.

This can result in a sudden burst of cross-region network traffic and disk I/O across all regions.

Region recovery needs to be controlled so that it doesn't overwhelm the healthy part of the cluster.

This can be achieved by throttling the replica catch-up, with the trade-off of longer recovery time to minimize the impact on live production traffic.

Replication throttling needs a deeper discussion of its own, so we won't go into details here.

The key point is that bringing a failed region back online is not simply a matter of restarting its brokers. We need to make sure that the recovery process itself doesn't impact the business.

Before putting a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster into production, validate these scenarios:.

There is no shortage of ways to deploy Kafka across multiple regions. The challenge here is to pick the right architecture that addresses all our durability guarantees.

For Tier-0 workloads, this means designing the architecture around failures first.

It has been revealed that what happens when a region goes down? Can we still roll the cluster? What continues to work, and at what point do we deliberately stop accepting writes?

Lastly, can we safely bring back the region that was down without impacting the business?

That is ultimately the difference between simply running Kafka across multiple regions versus actually supporting a mission-critical Tier-0 workload.

Continuous batching from first principles

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • In a recent development, if you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
  • This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

In a recent development, if you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one new token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many users simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

The attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

This is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

According to recent reports, consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a latest conversation starts here.

Industry observers note that each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

Input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

We then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

Recent findings suggest that finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

In a recent development, why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

After applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

Recent findings suggest that for example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

Recent findings suggest that the last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

The process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one latest token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

To compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

This follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

It has been revealed that moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

Recent findings suggest that in the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Recent findings suggest that let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

It has been revealed that KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

In a recent development, up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

In a recent development, let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

We can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

In our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

It has been revealed that to batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the fresh token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

Industry observers note that where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

It has been revealed that the drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Industry observers note that instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Sources indicate that furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

But we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

Although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

In the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with latest chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

By removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent consumers efficiently.

Industry observers note that in the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a fresh image generation and editing model.
  • According to recent reports, FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely new model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a fresh image generation and editing model.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

Industry observers note that first, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

Recent findings suggest that none of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

Sources indicate that A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Users who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:.

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

Industry observers note that using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

Sources indicate that ⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

Sources indicate that the example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:.

According to recent reports, for GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

In a recent development, FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

Industry observers note that FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Sources indicate that being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

According to recent reports, many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

Ask anyone selling an old chain or a broken ring what they want to know, and it's one thing: what is this worth? A small calculator can answer that in a second, but most of the ones you find online get the details wrong. They ignore troy ounces, treat 14K as 58.5% one day and 58.3% the next, or show a "value" that no buyer will ever pay.

Industry observers note that in this tutorial, we'll build a gold value calculator that gets those details right. It runs on plain HTML and JavaScript, updates as the user types, works with a screen reader, keeps its state in a shareable URL and pulls a live spot price through a small Node.js endpoint. The calculation lives in one pure function, so we can test it in a few lines.

Every gold calculator comes down to three inputs: how much the item weighs, how much of that weight is actually gold, and what pure gold is trading for today.

In a recent development, purity is measured in karats, out of 24. A 14K ring is 14 parts gold and 10 parts other metals, so it's 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3% gold. You'll also see 14K stamped as "585", which is the hallmark many manufacturers use for the same alloy. For a calculator, the karat fraction is the safer default:.

Sources indicate that the second detail most tutorials miss is the unit. Gold spot prices are quoted in USD per troy ounce, which is 31.1035 grams, not the 28.35-gram ounce on a kitchen scale. Jewelers also use pennyweight (dwt), which is 1.5552 grams. If your calculator multiplies grams by a per-ounce price without converting, every result is wrong by a factor of 31.

Put together, the formula looks like this:.

For example, with gold at $2,400 per troy ounce, 10 grams of 14K gold contains 5.83 grams of pure gold, which is worth $449.85 at melt.

That $449.85 is the value of the gold content alone. Refiners and buyers pay a percentage of it, because refining, assaying and handling cost money. Depending on the buyer, the item and the market, the payout can sit well below melt value.

That gap is why good production tools separate the two numbers. A dedicated scrap jewelry gold calculator, like the one The Alloy Market offers, lets sellers estimate what their gold is worth from its weight and karat before they send anything in. Our calculator does the same job with a payout field: leave it at 100% to see melt value, or enter a buyer's rate to see a realistic offer.

Start with real form controls and a visible for each one. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types, and screen readers handle it inconsistently. The W3C forms tutorial covers the rules in detail.

A few choices here matter more than they look:.

Sources indicate that A little CSS gives touch-friendly controls. Keeping inputs at 16px (1rem) also stops iOS Safari from zooming in when a field gets focus.

According to recent reports, the biggest problem with most calculator snippets is that the math is buried inside an event handler, mixed with getElementById calls. You can't test it, and you can't reuse it on a server. Put the calculation and validation in their own module instead:.

It has been revealed that both functions take plain values and return plain values. They don't know a DOM exists, which means the same file can run in the browser, in Node.js and in your test runner.

Notice that we don't round inside the calculation. Rounding happens once, at display time. Rounding in the middle of a chain of multiplications is a classic way to end up a few cents off.

Sources indicate that now connect the form to the module. Listening for the input event on the form itself catches changes from every field, including the dropdowns, so there's no need to wire up each control separately.

With the markup, CSS and script in place, here's the finished calculator showing our 10 g, 14K example with an 80% buyer payout:.

Here's what this code is doing:.

Asking customers to type the spot price works, but prefilling it is friendlier. Don't call a metals price API straight from the browser, though. Your API key would be visible to anyone who opens DevTools, and every visitor would spend one of your API calls.

Instead, put a small endpoint in front of your price provider and cache the result. This example uses Express and the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later:.

Three things keep this endpoint dependable:.

On the page, the loadSpot() function from Step 3 fills the field and shows the time of the price. The field stays editable, so a seller who has a quote from a specific buyer can type that instead.

It has been revealed that A seller comparing offers might want to send their numbers to a family member, or come back to them tomorrow. Because every input has a name, turning the form into a query string is one line with URLSearchParams.

It has been revealed that the syncUrl() function in Step 3 runs on every change and uses history.replaceState instead of pushState, so typing doesn't fill the back button with dozens of entries. On load, restoreFromUrl() puts the values back. A link like this opens with the form already filled in:.

Sources indicate that this is also the progressive enhancement story. If JavaScript fails to load, the form still submits as a GET request. Your server can read the same parameters, import the same gold.js and render the result in HTML.

Sources indicate that because goldValue() is a pure function, testing it needs no browser and no mocks. Node.js ships with a built-in test runner, so there's nothing to install:.

Run it with node --test. (Add "type": "module" to your package.json so Node treats the files as ES modules.) The troy ounce test is the one worth keeping forever: if anyone "simplifies" the conversion later, it fails immediately.

A quick checklist for putting this calculator on a real store:.

A gold calculator looks like a ten-line script, but the details are what make it useful: converting troy ounces properly, separating melt value from payout, keeping the math testable and making the result accessible and shareable. The same pattern of a pure calculation module, a thin DOM layer and a cached server endpoint works for any calculator where the price depends on several inputs, from shipping estimates to currency conversion.

Mathematically, 14K is 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3%. Many manufacturers stamp 14K jewelry "585" and alloy it to that standard, so both numbers are common. Pick one, state it in the dropdown, and use it consistently.

Let the user choose. Most people weigh jewelry in grams, but spot prices are quoted per troy ounce, so the calculator should accept either and convert internally.

According to recent reports, yes. Drop Step 4 and let people type the spot price, or have a scheduled job write the current price into a static JSON file. Everything else runs entirely in the browser.
